faq.a: Rely on the clinical picture and request a repeat sample if possible.
faq.q: What is the first step when a specimen is poorly fixed?

faq.a: Look for caseating necrosis and Langhans giant cells in TB; sarcoidosis shows non‑caseating granulomas without necrosis.
faq.q: How do I differentiate TB granuloma from sarcoidosis on H&E?

faq.a: Yes, a positive rapid test supports malaria‑related splenomegaly, but confirm with peripheral smear when feasible.
faq.q: Can I use a rapid malaria test to explain a splenic lesion?

exam: What histological feature would you look for to confirm a diagnosis of Kaposi sarcoma — presence of spindle cells forming slit‑like vascular spaces with extravasated red cells.

A patient presents with a painless cervical lymph node; the H&E shows necrotising granulomas. Which stain would you order next and why — Ziehl‑Neelsen to detect acid‑fast bacilli, because TB is common in the region.

If the slide shows sheets of atypical lymphoid cells but immunohistochemistry is unavailable, how should you proceed — describe the morphology, correlate with clinical B‑symptoms, and arrange referral for flow cytometry when possible.
During the practical you see a hemorrhagic liver specimen; what red‑flag complication must you consider — hepatic rupture leading to intra‑abdominal bleeding requiring urgent surgical review.

A skin biopsy shows epidermal hyperplasia with eosinophilic infiltrate; which endemic condition is most likely and what treatment is first‑line — cutaneous leishmaniasis; start pentavalent antimonial if available, otherwise refer for cryotherapy.

How would you explain a false‑negative HIV rapid test in a patient with active malaria — malaria can cause transient immune suppression affecting antibody detection; repeat testing after malaria treatment.

What is the most appropriate immediate management for a patient with a large, necrotic breast mass causing ulceration — start broad‑spectrum antibiotics, arrange wound care, and expedite surgical excision.

When a specimen shows extensive necrosis but no organisms, what complication should you watch for — secondary bacterial infection leading to sepsis; monitor vitals and start empiric antibiotics if fever develops.
ai.title: Pathology Practical Examination
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: A concise guide for Year‑4 students to approach pathology practical spot exams in low‑resource settings. Covers definition, diagnosis, common causes, investigations and management with exam‑focused strategies.

b: Identify tissue type, lesion morphology and any special stains used
Correlate findings with the patient’s presenting problem
sections.p: Pathology practical exams test your ability to recognise disease patterns on specimens, slides and gross samples and to link them to clinical scenarios.

b: Infectious: TB, malaria, HIV‑related opportunistic infections, schistosomiasis
Neoplastic: Kaposi sarcoma, hepatocellular carcinoma, cervical cancer
Traumatic/vascular: sickle‑cell vaso‑occlusion, rheumatic heart disease lesions
sections.p: In East African hospitals the most frequently examined specimens arise from infections, endemic malignancies and trauma.

b: History of fever, weight loss, or local pain guides differential diagnosis
Physical signs (e.g., hepatomegaly, skin nodules) narrow the list
sections.p: Patients are usually admitted with a focal complaint that matches the tissue examined – e.g., a painless lymph node, a skin ulcer, or a haemorrhagic stool.
Select tests that answer the key clinical question when the specimen is unavailable or when confirmation is needed.

t.b: Is a bacterial infection present? – Shows Gram‑positive or Gram‑negative organisms; if unavailable, use bedside pus microscopy.
Is acid‑fast bacilli present? – Detects Mycobacterium tuberculosis; if not possible, send sputum for GeneXpert.
What is the tissue architecture and cell type? – Provides basic diagnosis; if slide quality is poor, rely on gross description.
Is the lesion malignant and what is its lineage? – Helps differentiate sarcoma from reactive proliferations; if unavailable, use clinical pattern.
Is a viral infection contributing? – Positive result directs to viral‑related pathology; if kits are lacking, use clinical risk assessment.

b: Rapidly expanding neck mass causing airway compromise
sections.p: Recognise features that demand urgent action beyond the practical exam.

b: Infection: start empiric broad‑spectrum antibiotics (e.g., ampicillin‑sulbactam) pending culture; add anti‑TB drugs if AFB seen.
Malignancy: refer for surgery or chemotherapy; consider palliative radiotherapy where curative options are limited.
Trauma/vascular: give analgesia, transfuse if needed, and arrange urgent surgical review.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide supportive care appropriate to the lesion.

b: Schedule clinic visit within 2 weeks for histology report.
Vaccinate against hepatitis B and provide insecticide‑treated nets to reduce endemic infections.
sections.p: Ensure patients return for result review and secondary prevention.

b: Granulomatous inflammation vs. neoplastic granuloma (e.g., sarcoidosis vs. lymphoma)
Benign vascular malformation vs. Kaposi sarcoma
sections.p: Distinguish common look‑alike lesions that appear similar on gross or microscopic examination.

b: Poor fixation may mask necrosis, leading to under‑diagnosis of infarction.
Cross‑reactivity in rapid serology can give false‑positive HIV in malaria‑endemic areas.
sections.p: Be aware of pitfalls in interpretation, especially in low‑resource labs.
